rounds.goodbye: Two bills, one catalog. Worth the trip.
rounds.subtitle: Down the steps and out to the end of the drive, because the mail won't walk itself in. A look at the sky while you're there, a word to the neighbor's cat, and back with two bills and a seed catalog that is, frankly, the reason you went.
rounds.title: The Mailbox

rounds.subtitle: You're out of milk, which is the excuse you were waiting for. Round the corner past the launderette's warm breath, the shop's bell, two words with the owner about the weather that isn't doing anything, and back before the kettle has even thought about cooling.
rounds.title: The Corner Shop

rounds.goodbye: Four up, four down. Present now.
rounds.subtitle: The elevator is a fine invention and you are ignoring it. Four flights up the echoing stairwell — the door that sticks on three, the landing window with the water towers in it — and four back down, arriving at the next call with actual blood in your face.
rounds.title: The Stairwell

rounds.subtitle: The bag of bottles has been by the door since Thursday, judging you. Down to the containers on the corner — green, brown, white, a clank for every bottle and a small satisfying violence in each — and back the long side of the block because the evening is doing something with the light.
rounds.title: The Recycling

rounds.subtitle: The next one starts on the quarter hour, which leaves exactly enough time to walk the block and come back as a person. Out the door without the phone, around the corner where the wind lives, past the café you're not stopping at, and in again with the notes actually read.
rounds.title: Between Meetings

rounds.subtitle: The office coffee exists and that's all that can be said for it. The good place is two blocks up, and up is the operative word — the hill that makes the cup cost a little more than the price. Two flat whites, the walk back down with them level, the day negotiable again.
rounds.title: The Coffee Run

rounds.subtitle: The fridge has a lemon in it and nothing else, and the konbini three corners away is lit like a small sun. Down the sleeping street, the automatic door's chime, an onigiri chosen with real deliberation, and the walk back under a sky the color of a screen on standby.
rounds.title: The Konbini

rounds.subtitle: The bins go out Tuesday, and the whole street knows it — the roll of wheels on paving from every drive at once. Yours to the kerb, then a lap of the block because the night is mild and a fox is doing the same round, more professionally.
rounds.title: Bins Out

rounds.subtitle: Not the big walk — the dog knows the difference and forgives you. The short loop: the lamppost with the news on it, the hedge with the other dog in it, the corner where a sit is required for reasons no one has explained, and home with everybody's box ticked.
rounds.title: The Dog's Short One

rounds.goodbye: The pretend one was for you.
rounds.subtitle: Before the queue gets serious. Down the street with the shutters still half-drawn, the smell reaching you a whole block out, and the woman who already knows it's four Schrippen and one thing you'll pretend was for someone else. Home with the bag warm against your chest.
rounds.title: The Bakery

rounds.subtitle: The loop of the neighborhood, the one you could walk blind. Past the house with the flag and the one with the trampoline, the dip where the deer cross, the rise at the end where the mountains sit — going pink now, then violet, on schedule.
rounds.title: The Cul-de-sac

rounds.subtitle: Dinner is a sandwich and the sandwich is at the bodega, where the cat sleeps on the chips and the guy already knows the order. Down the avenue in the tail end of the day, past the stoop committee, the bell, the wait, and back up with the bag swinging.
rounds.title: The Bodega

rounds.subtitle: The paper could arrive by itself, but then you'd miss the walk to the kiosk — the frost still on the bike seats, the station coffee smell, the cashier's exact 'hej hej.' Back with the paper folded under your arm like someone in a film about being organized.
rounds.title: The Kiosk

rounds.goodbye: One memo, mostly wind. The good part's in there.
rounds.subtitle: The idea won't come at the desk; it never does. Out the door with the phone held like a walkie-talkie, talking to yourself in full sentences, the one good thought arriving at the corner exactly as you knew it would. Seven minutes, one memo, mostly wind.
rounds.title: The Voice Memo

rounds.goodbye: Can: opened at the bottom. Timing.
rounds.subtitle: At the top of the hill there's a vending machine that does the hot cans, and that is reason enough to climb it. Up the stepped lane past the tiled roofs, the coins in your glove, the clunk, the can warming both hands — and the walk down while it's still too hot to open.
rounds.title: The Vending Machine

rounds.goodbye: Two laps. One hot chocolate. Even.
rounds.subtitle: The outdoor rink is lit and full and you're not skating, you're walking the loop around it — the boards, the scrape of blades, someone's kid falling over with total commitment. Around twice in the cold, the hot chocolate hut a promise for the second lap.
rounds.title: The Rink Loop

rounds.subtitle: An actual letter, with a stamp on it, which means the postbox at the far end of the road — the one with the last collection you can still make if you go now. Down past the terraces and the cherry that's always early, the clunk of the slot, and back the sunnier side.
rounds.title: The Postbox

rounds.subtitle: The recipe wants lemons and the store is at the top of the hill, which the recipe did not mention. Up the block that leans, past the cable slot humming under the street, the corner store's cat, and down again with two lemons and the sort of breathing you'd normally schedule.
rounds.title: Up for Lemons

rounds.subtitle: The bus is eleven minutes away and the next stop is nine on foot, so the maths is done. Along the road with the frost in the ditch, the school kids on bikes in all weather, the fjord opening on the left like it's being cued — and the bus pulling in exactly as you arrive, as if that were the plan.
rounds.title: The Next Stop

rounds.subtitle: The block, the whole block, the way you'd show it to a visitor: the Späti with the bench, the playground going quiet, the courtyard with the chestnut, the corner where someone's always fixing a bike. Nothing to buy, no one to meet. Just the neighborhood, checked on.
rounds.title: The Kiez Loop

rounds.subtitle: The store that has the thing is two avenues over, and avenues are long. Crosstown with the wind funnelled between the buildings, the light that turns red the moment you reach it, the walk-signal shuffle — and the thing, when you get there, exactly as described. Rare.
rounds.title: Two Avenues Over

rounds.goodbye: Ten minutes at ditch speed. Recalibrated.
rounds.subtitle: Behind the houses the irrigation ditch runs its own straight line through town, and there's a path along it that nobody put on a map. Cottonwood fluff, a heron standing very still about its business, the mountains at the end of every cross street. Back in ten with the ditch's pace in your legs.
rounds.title: The Ditch Path

rounds.subtitle: The email is drafted and the draft is a mistake. Out before the send button gets braver — around the block once for the anger, once for the sentence you'd actually say, and a third time for nothing, because by then the point has made itself. Home. Delete draft.
rounds.title: Walking It Off

rounds.subtitle: Towel over the shoulder, coins in the pocket: the walk to the bathhouse is half the bath. Down the shopping street closing up, past the lantern, the ticking chimney coming into view — and you already warm from the walk, so the water only has to finish the job.
rounds.title: The Sento

rounds.subtitle: The lake is at the edge of town, which in this town means eleven minutes. Along the path with the reeds, the jetty where someone's already swimming in a temperature that's a personal choice, the light lying flat on the water. Turn at the bench. Nothing decided, everything better.
rounds.title: The Lake Path

rounds.subtitle: Down the steps to the towpath and the city drops away to canal speed — narrowboats, a moorhen, the smell of somebody's wood stove. Along to the lock, where a boat is going through and a small crowd has formed to supervise, and back up to street level with the hour defended.
rounds.title: The Lock

rounds.subtitle: Up to the top corner of the park where the whole city lays itself out for you — the palms, the downtown towers, the fog holding its line at Twin Peaks. The climb is the price of the view and everyone on the slope has paid it. Stand a minute. Then down the long side.
rounds.title: Dolores Corner

rounds.subtitle: The market is at the far end of the main street and so is everyone you know. Down past the hardware store and the good bench, into the stalls — the corn person, the honey person, the guy with the sourdough that sells out by ten — and back with more than the list and less than you wanted.
rounds.title: The Farmers' Market

rounds.subtitle: The train is 'delayed', which in this city is a mood, so you walk it — two stops along the tracks with the viaduct arches beside you, the bike shops and the Turkish bakery, the wind that lives under every bridge. You arrive as the train does. Naturally.
rounds.title: Two S-Bahn Stops

rounds.goodbye: The afternoon has a shape now.
rounds.subtitle: Down to the river because the office air has stopped being air. Across the highway on the light, out along the pier to the end where the wind is loudest and the ferries turn, one look at Jersey minding its own business, and back with the afternoon's shape decided.
rounds.title: The Pier and Back

rounds.subtitle: Along the wharf with the old warehouses gone gold in the low sun, the fishing boats tied up and ticking, someone hosing down a deck. The path follows the water to the point and turns you round — the town on the way back looking like the postcard of itself it's slightly embarrassed to be.
rounds.title: The Brygge

rounds.goodbye: "Talk next week." Same time, same loop.
rounds.subtitle: The weekly call, and you take it walking because sitting still for it makes you thirteen again. Around the neighborhood with one earbud in, the news from home — the neighbor's hedge, the cousin's new thing — and the pace settling to the rhythm of somebody else's stories. They know you're walking. They approve.
rounds.title: The Sunday Call

rounds.subtitle: One stop on the loop line is fourteen minutes on foot, and the train is full of everyone's day. Under the tracks with the yakitori smoke, along the backstreets that run parallel like a secret, past the tiny shrine wedged between two buildings — and up onto the platform at the next station as if you'd meant it.
rounds.title: Between Stations

rounds.subtitle: The short trail behind the neighborhood climbs to a bench that has the whole valley in front of it and the mountains behind. Steep enough to stop the day's thoughts, short enough that you're at the top before you've argued about it. Stand in the wind. Then the easy way down.
rounds.title: The Overlook

rounds.goodbye: Stopped for two dogs. Still made it.
rounds.subtitle: The far gate is fourteen minutes if you take the diagonal and don't stop for dogs, which you will. Across the grass still wet, the pond with the heron doing its statue act, the café's queue already forming — and out the other side into the day, which feels, briefly, optional.
rounds.title: Across the Common

rounds.goodbye: The city was kind. Note it.
rounds.subtitle: Along the water with the bridge coming and going in the haze, the ferry crowd streaming in, the old piers with their numbers, the sea lions somewhere off to the left making their views known. Flat, bright, and salted — fifteen minutes of the city being kind to you.
rounds.title: The Embarcadero

rounds.subtitle: The Sunday walk is not a plan, it's a condition. Out along the gravel path with half the town — prams, grandparents, a dog in a jumper — through the birches to the water and back, at the pace of people who have nowhere to be and are doing it properly.
rounds.title: Söndagspromenad

rounds.subtitle: Lunch eaten at the desk doesn't count as lunch; the loop does. Out the back way, past the place with the good bread, up the small rise where the wind finds you, around the square where the pigeons run the show, and back in with the second half of the day arranged.
rounds.title: The Lunch Loop

rounds.subtitle: Up the ramp with the tourists and the cyclists ringing at them, the boards under your feet, the cables opening overhead like the inside of a harp. The crown, the wind, the whole harbor at once — and down the other side into a borough that thinks it's the real one.
rounds.title: The Bridge

rounds.subtitle: The park has a hill the city built out of the war's rubble and grew over with trees until it was just a hill. Up the paths under the beeches, the flak tower's stone at the top with the view over the rooftops, and down the other side through the rose garden where the retirees have the benches under control.
rounds.title: The Volkspark

rounds.goodbye: The tram passed you twice. Fine.
rounds.subtitle: The tram would take nine minutes and you'd learn nothing. Under its wires instead — the old wooden houses in their colors, the bakery you'll go into next time, the hill the tram grinds up and you take at your own pace — arriving with the whole neighborhood's evening in your pockets.
rounds.title: The Tram Line Home

rounds.subtitle: For two weeks the avenue is gold — the ginkgos on both sides, the leaves down on the pavement like coins, everyone with a phone out and no one apologizing for it. Walk the whole length and back, slowly, because this is the fortnight and the rest of the year is just waiting for it.
rounds.title: The Ginkgo Avenue

rounds.goodbye: Wind switched sides. So did you.
rounds.subtitle: The lake is an ocean that forgot to be salt, and the path along it goes on further than you'll ever need. Out past the marina and the beach volleyball, the freighter on the horizon not moving, the tower doing its light show behind you — and back with the wind switching sides.
rounds.title: The Lakeshore

rounds.subtitle: The hill is small and knows it, which is why the whole city fits on top of it. Up the path past the dog walkers and the couple having the conversation, to the summit where the skyline is spelled out in a low stone rail — St Paul's, the Eye, the towers — and down into the streets that are all pastel and money.
rounds.title: Primrose Hill

rounds.subtitle: The old army post is a forest now, with a trail that ducks in and out of the eucalyptus and keeps handing you the bridge — there, gone, there again. Up through the cypress with the fog moving through it like smoke, a battery to stand on, and down past the bluff where the wind is a fact.
rounds.title: The Presidio

rounds.subtitle: The reservoir lies flat and bright under the foothills, and the loop around it is the town's living room after dinner. Runners, a paddleboarder going nowhere, the family with the slow dog, the mountains taking their time going dark. All the way round, and the last bit into the sunset on purpose.
rounds.title: The Reservoir Loop

rounds.subtitle: Over the bridge and up into the heights, where the city stops being tidy and starts being interesting. The water on both sides with the light going brass, the climb up the old steps, the cliff path with the whole roofline across the harbor — and a coffee at the end that you've walked far enough for.
rounds.title: Across to Söder

rounds.subtitle: Above the town there's a ridge, and above the ridge there's nothing, which is the point. The track climbs through the pines and out onto the bare rock, the wind arriving as the trees stop, the fjord below going all the way to its islands. A thermos at the cairn. The whole way down at the pace of someone who's had a thermos at a cairn.
rounds.title: The Ridge

rounds.subtitle: The short way is nine minutes and you know it too well. The long way takes you past the school with the murals, the street with the good trees, the house with the piano you've never seen anyone play, and along the water if there's water — and it hands you back your evening at the door, lightly used.
rounds.title: The Long Way Home

rounds.subtitle: Twenty blocks is a mile, a mile is twenty minutes, and the subway is right there being ignored. Up the avenue with the city changing every five blocks — the delis, the doormen, the church that shows up out of nowhere — the cross-street light doing its strobe thing, and the door of where you're going arriving at exactly the block it promised.
rounds.title: Twenty Blocks

rounds.subtitle: The mountain in the living room, taken properly: the gravel path switchbacking up under the maples, joggers in both directions, the stairs that appear when the path gives up. At the top the chalet's terrace hands you the whole city — the river, the bridges, your own street somewhere in it — and the way down is all momentum and Sunday.
rounds.title: Up to the Chalet

rounds.subtitle: Twenty minutes from the office there's a lot with three Subarus in it and a trail that starts climbing before you've locked the car. Up through the ponderosas with the sap smell, the first switchback for the head and the second for the legs, the ridge where the plains open out — and back down with the whole afternoon's argument already settled.
rounds.title: The Trailhead
